Review:
While I have a mountain bike and a road bike, I had been considering getting something like this - basically a cyclo-cross bike.

It's intended to ride longer distances primarily on pavement, but allows you to go on dirt roads or trails. In this case, the 28" wheels give you a definite advantage over ruts and bumps, though the lack of a front shock will be a definite limit if you try to go on more than fast single-track.

The components are the 7-speed Shimano Tourney with 2 chainrings and 7 cogs for 14 speeds - range isn't bad, though the steps are a bit wide. Tourney is the absolute bottom level mountain bike component group in the Shimano hierarchy, but I was pleasantly surprised that it functioned smoothly. The issue with the lower component groups is durability, adjustability and repairability. As long as you aren't too rough on your bike, this is more than enough for the average recreational rider who might be doing a 10 mile ride a couple of times a month, or who is commuting 2-3 miles each way. While I ride a lot more, I have a more serious mountain bike exclusively for trails and a road bike for long distances, so this is more for riding around the neighborhood where there are several grass, dirt, and gravel paths to cut through.

The disc brakes are mechanical meaning that there is a cable going to the disc calipers instead of hydraulic tubes. While this is a less expensive version, I actually don't mind too much because while it doesn't work as well as the hydraulic systems, you can't blow a seal and lose all brake function either.

One thing I would have preferred is a proper seatpost allowing more tilt adjust - this would allow you to rotate the seatpost and move the seat farther forward . The standard seating position is fairly far back from the pedals which is a more relaxing riding position when riding on the tops of the handlebars, but I prefer to be more forward for less strain on my back when on the drops (the lower side of the handlebars) then

The front rack is very solid, and lugs are provided for a rear rack. The stow sack under the top tube is a bit gimmicky, but at least it doesn't
One of the trickier parts of assembling a bicycle is setting the brakes - with disc brakes however, that is a complete non-issue. Being pretty handy with bicycles it took me less than 20 minutes to set up, if you're not familiar, there are plenty of how to setup new bike videos on YouTube.

Review: Was looking for a complete race ready bike with quality components for $400-$600. After some shopping around and reading reviews this one seemed to be the best deal. It arrived quickly with no damage or missing parts. It’s mostly assembled and the rest of the assembly is rather easy with some basic tools most everyone has at home. After looking over the quality of the parts and taking It out on a few rides I’d say this is an excellent bike that’s basically ready to race right out of the box. I gave it a 4 but it’s probably more like a 4.5 but that’s not an option. The deduction is for 5 issues I had 4 of which are mostly minor complaints. 1st issue I had was the brake handle. It’s really long like you’d see on a motorcycle. Besides being a little unnecessary added weight it’s also something that could get bent or broken in a crash or perhaps caught on another rides pants or shirt in a close racing situation. It works fine but I will be replacing it. 2nd the seat pole is too short for casual street riding. It’s padded for street riding but way too short and at a funny angle. The should’ve either made it slightly longer or just saved putting padding on It that’s just more added weight that’s unnecessary. 3rd issue is the chain seems pretty flimsy and cheap. It works fine again and may be no issue for most people but it too will be replaced. 4th issue is being an aluminum frame they should’ve included chain tensioners. Any ruder that rides hard is going to have issues with the chain creeping up which could lead to a popped chain plus It will shred the hell out of the aluminum when It does. This was noted by many others and I resolved it by ordering the tensioners at the same time I ordered the bike. The 5th and last issue was the only one that I’d consider a major issue. The pedals that come with the bike are complete junk. They’re plastic and don’t spin freely at all. I was never going to use the stock pedal anyway as I have clipless pedals but nobody should use those pieces of junk. Just expect to buy pedals for this bike if you don’t already have an extra pair. They really should use a better set of metal platform pedals on a race bike designed for a larger rider. One other thing for taller riders the top tube on the Pro XL is only 21.25” instead of the usual 21.5” so if you’re over 5’11” you’ll probably want to go with the Pro XXL. Overall this is a great bike for this price definitely an incredible value and I would recommend It to anyone looking for a ready to race bike that won’t break the bank. Can buy It on the 6 month EZ pay plan for only around $90 a month which is what I opted to do. Hope the review wasn’t too long and was helpful.

Review:
[[VIDEOID:f1872989bfa1adc05eff7ccc700cb2bd]] 5/19/21 Edit: WOW, the price has increased by $100 or 62.5% in under a year. Granted, that is for the "updated" model but there is no description what that means. The standard model is not available. Not cool.

Note: I paid the full $160 for this bike, it was not a free promotion in exchange for a glowing review. I just love bikes and I think this is a great niche item for some people. Amazon initially said 1-2 months for delivery (?) but happily it only took 5 days. It's out of stock at idshomeusa website, so Amazon may be the only source for these bikes now.

This bike just came yesterday, so I can't comment about reliability yet. But first impression is: I REALLY like this bike, it's an amazing value! This makes 15 bikes in my garage, including numerous other folding bikes (AKA "Folders"), some are Dahons. This "unYOUsual" bike has a curved main tube and is styled much like my $700 Dahon Mu P24, and I think it looks great. The bike is painted black with green trim stickers. Out in the sun, you can see that there are actually green metal flakes in the black paint. Really nice touch!

Of course it's NOT a Dahon, and I knew that going in. This is a no-name steel Chinese clone bike and I had low expectations. Very likely, quality varies between bikes. I do all my own bike repairs and adjustments, so I expected some work would be required to dial the bike in, and I was right. This bike "is what it is". It's mostly steel and will eventually rust, faster or slower depending on your environment and care. This bike would be a poor choice to leave outside or keep on a sailboat. Most parts are either not upgradeable or not worth upgrading. I'd call this a great kid's bike, or for an adult, a fine weekend bike or one to keep in the trunk of your car for fair weather use, moreso than a hardcore commuter bike through daily rain and mud. From my experience, it pays to manage your expectations up front. Folding bikes bring pluses and minuses to the table.

UPS delivered my bike-in-a-box in good shape, with just a few minor paint scrapes. The cardboard shipping box had a split in it, so the paint damage could have been much worse, not worth returning IMO since there were no dents, damage and everything else was fine. Both wheels spun nice and true (no wobbling). Aluminum rims good, plain steel spokes bad (you want stainless). Plain steel spokes will rust/corrode eventually. (My single-speed Dahon boardwalk also has plain steel spokes, which have light oxidation after 12 years, always stored in the garage.) The "Wanda" tires look good and are supple and grippy. Tires say "Inflate to 43 PSI", which is a very low pressure rating. Better tires can handle higher pressure for less rolling resistance.

Both brakes and shifters required adjustment for proper function. Easy enough for me, but probably not for everyone. No special bike tools are required, just an adjustable wrench (or socket set), a Phillips screwdriver and a metric Allen wrench set. After centering via adjustment screws, the brakes work great, don't rub and are very quiet. Brake levers (handles) are aluminum, while the V-brake arms are steel. 6-speed Shimano grip shifter & derailleur work fine after careful adjustment. The 14-28 freewheel (not cassette) gives a nice gear range and replacements are widely available. The chain was clean and came with a light layer of lube on it. High gear on this bike matches pedal cadence & bike speed of a single-speed beach cruiser. Low gear is exactly half of that, suitable for some moderate hill climbing. Steel crank arms are 170 mm long. The non-folding pedals are easy to install if you know that the left pedal uses a left hand thread. The pedals do not spin freely (yet), they feel like the cheapest part on the bike.

The handlebar is a welded aluminum T: you can't change it but it works fine. It telescopes to adjust the height into a steel tube which hinges to fold down. The locking mechanism feels very solid, and lock tension is adjustable using two small Allen wrenches (photo). My headset (steering shaft bearings) came adjusted properly, no binding and no excess play. I rotated both brake levers and the grip shifter on the bar to my ergonomic preference using an Allen wrench. A bell and front reflector are included to mount on the handlebar using a Phillips screwdriver.

The seat is comfortable and came pre-mounted at the right angle on the long and large diameter steel seatpost. A red rear reflector for the seatpost is included. The seatpost has a diamond knurling pattern for the quick release adjuster to grip. There is a "Maximum height" line engraved. I'm 6'-0" and the right seat height is a half-inch above the max line. In my experience there no danger, there is plenty of seatpost left in there. I weigh 190 pounds and the bike feels solid and responsive, quite similar to my more expensive Dahons.

No tools are required to fold the bike or adjust seat and handlebar height. Both adjusters and both folding mechanisms (main tube and handlebar) feel solid. The wide range of height adjustments allows a folder like this to fit nearly anyone, I'd say from 4-1/2 feet to my 6 feet. My 11 year old is 5 feet tall and she has a blast riding this bike. Folding this bike is straightforward if a bit clunkier than my Dahon. The folded size is similar, except the pedals don't fold. It weighs ~32 pounds, 8 pounds more than the Dahon Mu (steel vs aluminum).
A few nice surprises: The rear-mounted kickstand has a locking feature to it, you kick the middle black lever, not the bottom of the kickstand. The bike has dropouts (mounting holes) for an optional rear rack.

Riding the bike is delightful and fun. It is smooth and responsive in all ways. Brakes and shifter (after adjustment) work great to deliver a pleasant experience. Note that 20" wheel bikes (Dahons included) have a different feel and more rolling resistance than bikes with larger wheels, say 26" or 700C. More pedaling effort is required, and the small wheels may feel twitchy to first timers. After some practice, "twitchy" becomes nimble and maneuverable.

Review:
I picked up the World DBX on a closeout and I'm very glad I did. I had been looking at some comparable bikes with similar features and they were twice or more what I paid. The genius of the bike is the rear caliper being mounted inside the rear triangle instead of outside which is standard. This allows standard rack and fenders to be mounted without having to go the disk special type racks.

The Avid BB7's disc brakes work great. I've got discs on my mountain bike and I don't think I'll ever go back to canti's again. The braking modulating is better than typical brakes and the rim getting hot is not an issue. Although, the rotors do get hot and it doesn't take much to get them hot. I got a nice singer on the leg after testing the brakes on a small downhill and then straddled the front wheel adjusting the handlebars afterward.

The inline brake handles are a great feature. It's easier and more natural to go from the hoods to the tops than the hoods to the drops for those with a mountain bike history. The caveat is that they eat up valuable bar space. After adding the bracket for my handlebar bag, I'm out of room to mount any lights or a computer. So I'll be picking up a bar extender/swing bar soon for the lights. Not sure about the computer, but I don't know if I want one. My commute seems much more relaxed not knowing how fast I'm going.

The components are fair to good. 105 rear derailer, tiagra front and tiagra sti shifters. The 105 rear handles the 9 cog rear with ease. I think the tiagra front suffices, but I might switch it out for an upper model. Same for the shifters.

I've read elsewhere that the wheels are very low end and heavier than a good wheel. I don't know really care as long as they last and are issue free. This isn't a race bike and I'm not counting oz.'s.

The fenders are a nice touch and have made a difference on my commute. Even though I'm technically in the desert, there's enough surface water to splatter things up nicely from sprinklers and water trucks spraying to keep dust down

The tires seem sufficient. I'm glad the bike can handle wide cycecross tires and I'll be taking some of those on my mountain tour next month. I'll also be upgrading to a more beefier tire for commuting. Continental Gators probably.

The pedals are clipless on one side and platform on the other. A great feature. However, I'm in love with my Powergrips and swapped those in. I'll probably go more clipless once I break my new shoes in on the mountain bike.

The gearing is sufficient. 27 speeds. 50/39/30 up front. 12-26 in the rear. If that isn't sufficient, a touring group up front might be better. I might go that route when I do more tour next month.

The bike has more heft than a lot of bikes and comes in at 23 lbs or so. But that's still lighter than most mountain bikes. And for a commuter, it's no big deal. The carbon fork helps with weight. I just hope it's durable.

Overall, I couldn't happier with this bike as a commuter.

These have been discontinued so they won't be around for long. The new line are flat bar with internal hubs and less gearing options. That just doesn't work for long commute with hills, heat, and wind.

Review:
I was looking for a sturdy, well-made bike for my daughter's first bike. She's only three, but she's 40 inches tall, and I figured a 16 inch bike would be the best bet. The options at the box stores grabbed her attention with all the pretty princess and disney themes, but I was skeptical about the quality. I purchased the pink Bikestar, mainly due to it's stellar reviews on Amazon, but also because it has a sturdy metal rear rack (for her babies), a usable basket (not a silly plastic case-type thing), and a chain guard that covers the entire chain (you'd be suprised how many kids' bikes only have a partial chain guard).

Shipping from Dakota Cycle was super fast! Took only 3 days, which was good since I was only a week away from her birthday! The bike is easily assembled with basic tools and the instructions are very clear. I put it together on my lunch break.

As for the bike itself, it is a quality bike for sure. Well built, but not too heavy either. I couldn't be happier. Dakota Cycle will get my business again when my son is ready for one.

If I had to pick out a negative, it's the front reflector. The bracket is plastic, and will most likely break in the future, but it's not like my three-year-old will be doing any night rides, not to mention, the basket partially obscures it anyway.

It is significantly more expensive than the big box store bikes, and you'll have to shell out extra for training wheels, but the quality in this bike is well worth it. If you're like me, you don't mind paying more for quality, if it saves money in the long run. You won't regret buying this bike. Slap some princess stickers on it if you have to!

Review:
This bike far exceeded my expectations. I am primarily an in-city and path rider and have appreciated the performance on poorly maintained streets. I've purchased bikes locally for several hundred dollars more than this that have had worse components than this beauty. I followed the advice of several reviews and went ahead and purchased a more comfortable seat. At first the double clamp mount didn't seem large enough for the seat, but as I started to tighten the clamp onto the rails of the seat, the rails just seemed to fit themselves in. I also added a 9" kryptonite lock that fits comfortably mounted high on the inside of the frame toward the front tire without getting in the way (on a 20"/XL bike). The assembly instructions are not sequential, but are part-by-part and are all over the place. I chose the order to do things pretty incorrectly and often had to back-track. However, even without prior building or tuning experience, the documentation was sufficient to help me figure out how to build the bike and tune it to my exact preference. The brakes, derailleurs, and position of everything feel perfect now, which I have never done for myself before. In the end, the experience of working through the build was a definite gain in terms of my confidence to keep my own bike tuned.

All of the parts feel very solid, and the gears shift cleanly and without much noise (none from the rear derailleur, and a little from the front (Shimano) derailleur going up from first to second gear). The derailleurs most definitely need to be adjusted in order to work cleanly, so expect this extra slightly involved task. Also, the handles seem perhaps on the firmer side and my hands feel sore after a long ride even with heavy gloves on. I might go in for some soft handles come springtime.

Also, the snow can be pretty heavy here in Boston during the winter, and my road bike has an impossible time after a storm, but this bike handles moderate snow and ice well.

In all, I love this purchase and definitely trust this company! Also, to respond to a previous complaint I read about parts coming poorly packaged to where they were bent and/or scratched, I'd say that the manufacturer has perhaps responded the this because the packaging seemed sufficient and nothing came blemished (more than expected) or bent (at all).

Definitely purchase this bike if it's in your budget range.

Review:
I'm happy with this purchase. I bought it for my 8-year-old who wanted a bike with gears and handlebar brakes and has outgrown his single gear bike.

Overall, the assembly was easy. I didn't use the tool included with the bike and instead used regular tools. I find that makes things easier than trying to manage with a thin piece of metal that has unlabeled cutouts in place of wrenches. The hardware is metric, if that helps.

I appreciated that the brake lines were already attached and run; the brakes just had to be latched and adjusted. The gear line (it has one shifter) was also already attached and run, making assembly easier.

The difficult part was making adjustments, or rather, getting the adjustments right. I saw in other reviews people complaining about the brake levers being too far from the handle bar for a kid to reach the brakes. Those can be adjusted to be nearer the handlebar. Doing so is easy; however, you then have to adjust the associated brake itself so the tension isn't too tight or loose. That part is difficult because you have to loosen a nut, pull the brake line, and then tighten the nut without releasing the tension you just put in. It takes some trial and error, and I found using pliers to pull the brake line makes things a little easier.

Another note about the brake levers: they feel very flimsy when adjusted to be closer to the handlebar. I'm not sure what the lever is made out of (I think plastic), but that's not the issue: when adjusted close to the handlebar, the lever moves up and down at the joint and feels like it could snap off. I haven't had issues with it yet, but time will tell.

Review:
First, here are some stats:
The bike weighs 37 pounds
The seatpost height is 25 inches
The maximum (safe) pedal to seat height is 31.5 inches (which means if your inseam is 33" or taller, don't get this bike)

First things first--you SHOULD/NEED to get this bike professionally tuned/built when it arrives if you have NO experience working on bikes [.............]. I have worked in a bike shop for many years, so I know my way around a bike, and if you want this bike to work like a bike should, you need someone who knows what they're doing to tune/build it. (If you're wondering why I didn't get a bike at my old shop, it's because I moved across the country--don't work in a shop anymore).

Anyway, I have plenty of high-dollar bikes hanging in my garage, but I needed an upright ride because my back is going out on me. If you can tune/build/true your own bike or have a buddy who will do it for you, this is a great deal. Otherwise, you'll probably be better off going to your local bike shop and buying a bottom of the line brand name cruiser that has been properly built.

This bike was double-boxed and in pretty decent shape when it arrived with FedEx. There was a large paint gouge on the rear down-tube, but only superficial. The brake/derailleur cables were frayed because they didn't put cable fairings on the end. The wheels were rideable but out-of-true, and if you don't get them trued you will incur permanent damage and end up paying a whole lot more for new wheels.

All the bolts were there, except one for the rear fender (I just used a zip tie to secure it). It does not have holes in the downtubes to attach a rear rack, so you'll have to gerry-rig it. If I keep this bike, I'll throw a new rear derailleur on, but the one it came with will get you where you need to go. In my opinion this a great bike for the money. If you have a bike mechanic friend, buy him a six pack and you're set. If you are on your own, I'd suggest getting a cheap but well-put together bike at your local bike shop (NOT Target or Walmart--they don't have mechanics putting their bikes together).

My one BIG complaint about this bike is the size. I'm 6'1", and I figured it would be semi-small since it's one-size-fits-all, but it's actually quite a petite bike. I'm stretching the seat-tube past the recommended limit until I can buy a longer one. You don't want to pay [.............] for knee surgery to save [.............] on a bike, so if you're 5'11" or taller, find something cheap that comes in a large size.

Like I said, having worked in a shop, the frame and the parts are more or less on par with a low-end brand name cruiser bike, it's the labor that makes the price difference.

Review:
Overall, very good bike for the price. A couple things worth mentioning that are consistent with other reviews:
-The shipping packaging was almost non-existent; it is just a bike and a box, so depending on the carrier, some parts may be bent.
-I was missing the quick release bolt for the front wheel, but after calling Mongoose, they mailed me a new one no questions asked.
-If the wheel turns ~30 degrees, your toes will probably hit the tire while peddling unless you have the ball of your foot exactly on the center of the pedal. This seems common with 29" tires, but it seems like they could make the frame an inch or two longer so it isn't a problem... After some getting used to, it isn't much of a problem.
-Even though it is aluminum, it isn't a particularly light bike
-Even though it comes partly 'assembled', it is 0% adjusted, and you will need to fully adjust calipers/brakes/lines front and back, as well as all gearing. The manual is generic to all Mongoose bikes, so you need to find the section specific to yours. Once adjusted, everything works properly, but plan on taking a few hours to reach that point.
-The seat stem should be an inch or two longer. I am 6'1", and with the seat fully up, I still need a couple additional inches so that I have an efficient leg position.

Review: I recently purchased this bicycle for my wife after she had taken my 15 year old Dahon and would not give back to me.  The Mariner D8 is a lightweight, solid bicycle that folds down to a reasonably small package, making it a great commuter bicycle.  In addition, the fenders do a good job of keeping the mud streaks off of clothing and gear.  The gear ratio settings are about right, allowing for relatively steep grades to be climbed despite having a single chain ring in the front.  The bike tops out at around 25 mph with respect to gearing, but 30 mph can be achieved going downhill.  The 20" wheels are large enough to avoid flipping or getting caught in potholes, while still being small enough for the bike to fold into a tight enough package for traveling.  The fold down handlebar stem is much improved over my older generation of Dahon.  The Mariner D8 has also proven to have the same dependable reliability and high quality I have come to expect from Dahon.  I have looked at Brompton's and they are nice bikes, but it is hard to justify double the price difference for something that is of equal performance.  Kudos to Dahon for making great bicycles and continuing to iterate on solid engineering and building on quality.

Review:
This is a review of the Schwinn Comfort Bicycle, Model Suburban DLX.

Here our my thoughts and observations:

-Nice strong frame with good welds and nice finish.
-This is a heavier bike.
-Strong 6061 aluminum frame with limited lifetime warranty by Schwinn!
-Good attachment points and cable routing system.
-Frame also has attachment points for a bottle cage and rear rack system. Those items are not included.
-Nicely cushioned seat with built-in suspension post and quick-release lever for easy adjustments.
-Handlebars come with fully adjustable quill stem for easy height and angle adjustments.
-Handlebars have nicely padded grips.
-Brakes and shifters are comfortably positioned to the inside of the grips.
-Rear shifter is an indexed 7-speed twist-type shifter.
-Front chainring shifter is a 3-speed friction-twist shifter.
-Front and rear brakes are V-rim brakes.
-This is a hardtail frame with a non-adjustable front suspension fork.
-Tires are 27.5 x 2.4 inches with a nice center bead and good traction lugs to the outside, making this bike versatile for street or gravel/dirt roads and trails, such as rails-to-trails conversions.
-Both wheels are sturdy 36-spoke aluminum with a nicely finished braking surface.
-Front and rear wheels also have quick-release hubs for easy flat repair.
-This is a 7-speed rear cassette with a triple chainring up front, making the bike versatile for tackling hills or riding distances.
-All shifting and braking components are Shimano, which is great!
-The bike is made in China.

There are no assembly instructions included that are specific to this bike model. The average person should consider taking this bike to a shop for assembly and adjustments.

Overall, a well made bike for a good price! It should last quite a long time! Recommended! 5 stars!

Review:
If you are shopping for a nice road bicycle right now, like I, you have probably found out how hard they are to come by. I decided to buy this one because it was the best I could find for around $1,000.00.

The bike came quickly and as promised. No problem putting it together, although there were no instructions included in the box. Perhaps this is because they want you to take it to a bike shop? I'm not sure. Anyways, it took about an hour for me to put it together. Everything came wrapped in foam and the major sections were semi-pre assembled in the box.

Riding it I found that it is lighter feeling than my steel trail bike, but heavier than a full carbon-framed bike like a Trek. The frame is quite stiff too, so you won't want to ride this one on anything but a smooth road surface. I replaced the stock seat right out of the box with a more cushioned one I found here on Amazon. I also added a rear pouch, electric horn, two water bottles and some strapless toe clips, which were a huge safety and performance improvement.

The bike is very nimble too. It took some short test rides and adjusting to get the seat and handlebars where I wanted them. That was to be expected. The front deraillleur was a bit out of adjustment though, so it took some fiddling with to get it right and to get all of the gears indexed. The rear wheel was also out of true so I had to work on the spoke tensions a bit as well. The rear wheel also needed some oil on the rear hub assembly, as it was squeaking when it turned. I also oiled both of the deraillieurs and the chain.

All-in-all I'd say this bike is a 3 out of 5 stars. It is certainly as stated in the ad, but a little disappointing for the price tag. A good bike for someone who is just starting out on a true road bike though, not wanting to spend $2-5k. I can see that in a couple of years time that I might want to move up to something a little better though.

Review:
I bought this tricycle for my wife, a senior citizen, for Christmas. The bike arrived promptly. Unfortunately, one fender was broken. The seller replaced the one broken fender immediately with not one but three replacement fenders. Assembly is no problem for those mechanically inclined and the video on the Amazon website is helpful. For those less mechanically inclined, however, professional assembly is strongly recommended. It takes a bit of time and patience to put the tricycle together, but the effort is well worth it.

One issue is the saddle. The saddle tilts either forward or backward under the weight of a rider (my wife is only 110 pounds). Tightening the nuts further strips them. The ridges on the mating parts under the saddle as well as the bolt that secures the saddle to the stem are made from a very soft steel. The seller, though, once again, responded admirably and within a few days a replacement saddle, this time one with a backrest, which normally is an extra expense, arrived. Unfortunately, this saddle has the same issues. Rather than risking stripping the nuts again, after adjusting the saddle to the right angle, I spot-welded the mating parts, which resolved the issue. It prevents further angle adjustments to the saddle but front back and height adjustment still work. For those without access to a welder, a high-quality adhesive would likely do the trick as well, as would a stronger stainless-steel replacement nut and bolt from Home Depot, Lowes, etc. As stated, not a problem for someone mechanically inclined or even good problem-solving skills.

Overall, a very good bike for the price and a very responsive seller. It is recommended for everybody who wants a solid bike and does not mind one or the other initial set-up problem. Without these start-up issues the tricycle would deserve a 5* rating

Review:
Don't let the "low" price fool you - this bike is insane value.

I have never owned a Schwinn bike before, and I'm super impressed with what I have seen so far. Prior to getting this bike I had a really old Raleigh road bike and new Diamond Back mountain bike. For the last year, I spent the first 6 months on the road bike and the last 6 months on the mountain bike as I would navigate the 10 mile trails around the lake.

I have been using a Suunto Spartan Trainer watch and the Under Armor 'Map My Ride' app on my phone to monitor my stats. Because I have done the trail so often I know where I should be at 5, 10, 15, 20, 30, 35, and 40 minutes. Typically, it takes me right at 50 minutes to do the 10 miles, but the last few times on the new Schwinn, I am coming in at 48 minutes. The bike is super light which is so refreshing, but its weight is not light enough to take two minutes off my ride

It is an interesting discovery to see that the features that many people use to determine a purchase decision may not actually be the right selection criteria. I say that to say that my mountain bike has 24 gears and the new Schwinn only has 14. Initially I thought that this would be a step down - boy was I wrong...

The crazy thing is that I go faster with less effort on this bike. I know its all about ratios, but I don't understand going faster with less effort - that boggles the mind. I know the places on the trail where I would have to rise up off the seat to deliver more power to keep up with my son, but with the Schwinn I don't have to.

The seat is super comfortable, and without making any fit modifications other than seat height, this is perfection for my leg length etc.

I absolutely love the gear shift mechanism with the brake leaver integration, although it is a little difficult to brake and downshift at the same time. Not really an issue for me since I know the trails well and can plan in advance.

The only thing I am not too terribly keen on is that the brakes are no match for the disc brakes on my mountain bike, but A. That is an unfair comparison and B. I can always get different pads.

In closing - for the money this bike delivers huge value, and when I mentioned earlier about the low price, I am saying that in reference to the fact that you could spend that money on a range of other bikes even from lower price outlets like Walmart and never find your self enjoying this level of quality and craftsmanship.

If you are reading this review - go ahead and get yourself one :)

Review:
I'm not sure if they are calling this bike a "BMX" style because it has pegs, or because it doesn't have a foot brake, but that is about it. Call it what it is. It is a normal 1 speed bike. There is nothing wrong with that, just say what it is. When I was growing up, a BMX freestyle bike not only had foot pegs, but it had the front handlebar mechanism that allowed you to spin the handle bars 360 degrees with out the break wires getting in your way. You cannot do that with this bike because the rear break cable gets in the way.

So knowing this, this is what the bike is about. Its a single gear/speed. Does not have a foot break. It does have front and rear hand breaks. It does NOT come with a kickstand (that is a big con), and it does not have a quick adjust seat. You need an allen wrench to adjust the seat. (another big con). My BMX bike as a kid, we took the kick stand off when we were doing tricks so they don't get in the way, but since this is not a BMX style bike, it should have a kick stand.

Putting it together wasn't too bad. One of the bike pedal threads were screwed up so it took a lot of work to get the pedal on, but I eventually got it. Breaks were a pain to properly adjust.

In my opinion, this is a way over priced "normal" bike with out a kickstand or quick seat adjustment. You can get similar bikes from other places with the same or better quality and features for about half the price.

Give it a kick stand, quick seat adjustment, and reduce the price A LOT, then it becomes a 5 star bike.

Review:
We are replacing an old wooden balance bike, and one of the things that always bothered us about it was that every time I'd take it out after not using it for a while, the tires would be flat. I was so happy to see that the tires on this one are airless. Everything seems to be made of high quality materials, and assembly was quick and easy. Just slide in handlebars, fork, and front wheel, then tighten a couple of bolts with the included allen wrench. Seat adjustment does not require tools.

The sizing is similar to the three other balance bikes I have reviewed or bought at yard sales over the years (none brands you have heard of), so no surprises there in terms of heights of child who can ride this - seems pretty standard across the board. I like the curved seat which is super comfortable. I actually sat on it myself and it felt very comfortable despite my being an adult on a child's bike. Just the sort of effortless comfort I remember from my BMX bike when I was a child.

I know so many people recommend balance bikes over bikes with training wheels because it makes the transition to riding a proper bike so much easier, and it's easier to learn to balance on a pedal-less bike that you scoot on and direct with your feet. This is the nicest we have tried and I really like the steering, comfort of the seat, aforementioned airless tires, and the proportions.

Buyer Beware before purchasing . Battery is "Wartime New Energy Co. Ltd" with a model number of "WT0230" Search for replacement battery before purchasing 48v-10A model T-276 27&1/2 inch TotGuard ebike. ( I am still Looking for a replacement Battery . Battery Information should of been posted upfront on sellers page ( -1 star for lack of important information on "Advertisement Page"). The Computer for selecting power assist reads in highest power assist at 39.8mph while the same speed traveling in mid power assist selection reads it at 22mph. Big discrepancy in the reading of traveling speed. ( No star deduction for this as seller does provide a PDF file that attempts to explain how to set the computer control of the bike. Thank You Seller for this important information. ) . Front Forks are leaking. Like a motor cycle or any other motorized Bike, this posses a serious health risk to the rider. ( I contacted the seller and awaiting a response ). If the battery does not remove easily , make sure you turn the key counter clockwise to disengage the lock. You may have to step on pedal and use both hands to lift and pull the battery upwards towards the front of the bike. This is due to the mounting plate not being properly set in the plastic holder by the manufacturer before shipping to be sold. the mounting plate can be adjusted up or down by loosening the three Philips screws ( first check for marks on the mounting plate where the locking pin is binding. I have not adjusted mine yet, but I see marks where it looks like this plate was used or screwed on wrongly and then screwed on properly afterwards ) . I am wondering if the Brake switches are even wired in as when I engage the brakes , the motor continues to push me forward for 2 seconds before disengaging ( Yes I stop pedaling when I engage the brakes ) . I am looking over the PDF files to see if there is adjustments in the computer for that, just in case the wires are actually connected and it be the computer not set properly . I will update my review about Seller's response on bad front forks and if and when I can find a replacement battery. as for the PDF instructions I need to read more concerning the computer settings. over all though, it does not seem like a bad bike.

Update :
Seller Responded quickly within 24 hours. Leaky Forks is just excess grease packed around the Sweeps of the forks. I would suggest to anyone that has never rebuilt the forks on their bike to watch some videos on it. At some point the seals are going to need replacing along with replacing of the oil inside . Although I am still surprised that the sweeps allow grease to slip by. If this was a motor cycle I would be very concerned. The PDF the Seller provides on the lower part of the page was handy for setting up the computer .
I find the front drive train to be a little to small when in power assist . I prefer to pedal a little slower with applying a little more leg power at a steady pace. I Noticed 2 days ago that the TotGuard Ebike official site was completely gone ( that is a bit concerning, So no help support can be relied upon by TotGuard.)

Brakes are another thing which there is no markings on what the brakes are in order to determine which brake pads fit it . Battery is still a mystery . Review:
I have been a life long bicycle rider - with a brief hiatus for about 10 years. I'm 47 now. My wife and I had nice road bikes that we stopped using when we moved to a place with lots of hills.
We moved again... and they got stoled out of or yard. Boooo!

I've been on the prowl for a replacement bike for a while when I was turned onto the One-Wheel. It looks nice but with a price tag of $2,000+ - no way. I was intrigued by it's electric power when I had the bright idea of getting an electric bike. I had seen a couple go by in my neighborhood and they looked fun, and fast.

Now with gas prices going up as much as they are my big V8 truck was costing me a lot of money to just run errands around town. My hardware store is only 2 miles. Honestly, I can get to Safeway and back faster than in my truck because I don't have to park and go in (I pull my bike inside) and as soon as I leave the door, my fancy electric bike will whisk me away, no walking back to my parked vehicle, no waiting for traffic.

Shipping: It shipped very fast and I had my bike in only a few day.

Assembly: I know bicycles, so assembly was very quick as nearly everything is preassembled - it's just taken apart for shipping. Handlebars on, front wheel on, attach pedals, connect connections, tighten all allen heads for safety and your ready to go - as soon as you charge the battery. Very simple.
ALL the tools you will need for assembly are included. As well as some you won't need unless you are servicing the bike and need metric tools.

Instructions: Poorly worded instructions translated into English. Pics are so-so. But if you know anything about bicycles, it's a breeze.

Size: The bike is a real nice size. I am 5' 11" and it fits me well. My wife is shorter, 5' 6", and she can stand over the top bar no problem.
I like how the handlebars are adjustable up for someone who wants to sit taller.
I also like how the brakes have pre-threaded holes for a mirror or accessory that can thread into the brakes.
I like how the brakes are - Left hand, front. Right hand, back. I have another bike that is reversed and i do not like it at all.

Overall impression: I love it. Cruise around pedaling with 15% of the effort of cycling. Or use the throttle and don't pedal at all, just coasting along quietly.

My very first ride was from my town to the next town - about 7 miles one way. I had charged the bike the night before and was ready to go the next morning. I had not cycled ANY in over 10 years and I was wondering how I would do on this long ride. I did consider cancelling, but I was optomistic and went for it. Not sure of the battery life (although it's specified in the description) I pedaled there on medium. It was an easier ride than I've every had. I did my business in town, stopped to say "Hi!" to my Mom and show off my new toy, and was back on the road for the ride back. My battery still showed full - so I decided to return home with the bike on High and see what it could do. - IT. WAS. AWESOME. Never before had I made that ride so quickly and I was not more than slightly winded after pedaling the entire way back. Ok, not the entire way, when I got tired I twisted the throttle to keep my speed, and rested my legs. It was quick and easy.

I highly recommend this bike. U wanna get somewhere without using your vehicle? This is it. Get some sunshine! Get outside! Feeling tired... no problem! This bike has your back and will take you where you want to go with just a twist of the throttle or a spin of the pedals.

Review:
I bought the 18" version for my 7 year old son who is around 46" tall. It fits him well with what looks like plenty of room to grow. Like other reviews have said, this is a high quality bike for the money. It looks great, and I think the weight is very reasonable. I picked this model (with the aluminum frame) to save a couple of pounds. The water bottle, cage, and bell are nice extras and the front caliper brake is a nice introduction to hand brakes for him. It was easy enough to put together. And my son loves it, so overall it's a win.

However, just like other reviewers have noted, there are some problems to be aware of:

1. I needed my own wrenches to really crank down on the nuts that hold the pedals onto the crank arms. Couldn't get enough leverage with the supplied tool to keep the right pedal from falling off.

2. The front brake was not adjusted correctly from the factory. It was rubbing on the rim and making the bike harder to ride. I needed to adjust it to keep it from constantly rubbing on the rim. It's now easy for him to reach and modulate.

3. The front wheel is not true. But this isn't a really big deal (I think).

4. The chain was way too tight from the factory. This was making the bike much harder to ride than it should it have been. After adjusting it, the bike was much easier to ride (and quieter). The chain will probably last longer now also.

5. When brand new, the crank is tight. Once again, making it harder to ride. After about 10 miles or so, it loosened up and became easier pedal.

6. The pedals don't really spin as easily as they should. This probably makes the bike a little harder to ride than it should be. I don't think I can do anything about this however.

After making the adjustments above, the bike became a lot easier for my son to ride. Before I adjusted the chain and the front brake, he was tired after 3-4 miles of relatively easy biking - not much fun for him. Now he has no trouble with 10 or more miles.
